name: impulse-bounce
title: Impulse bounce
summary: A ball dropped at start that bounces three times and rests: a 3-second impulse draws the bouncing ball, and a condition draws it at rest afterwards.
prompt: Animate a ball that drops when the widget appears, bounces three times and then rests on the ground.
teaches: Run a one-shot animation window with impulse(duration, start) and draw inside it with impulseProcess
Bounce with |cos(π·t)| scaled by a decay (1 - t/3)² that reaches zero when the impulse ends
Draw the resting state after the window with conditionalOperations gt animationTime() 3
Fit a drawing authored at the header size to any box: a variable s = min(componentWidth() / W, componentHeight() / H), a translate by half the extra space and a scale by s about the design's centre

snippets.note: impulse 3 s from 0, its process draws the ball at the bounce height
after 3 s, the ball at rest on the ground

check.describe: After 1 s of frames the ball is in the air at the top of its first rebound (y ≈ 155); after 5 s it rests on the line (y = 244). Resized, the ball, its drop and the floor scale together to fit and stay centred.

pitfalls: An impulse runs its plain commands on the first frame of its window and its impulseProcess only on later frames, so a single still frame draws nothing from the process: render with `duration` to simulate frames
Nothing is drawn by the impulse outside its window: draw the final state yourself (here a conditionalOperations on animationTime() > 3), or the ball vanishes when the bounce ends
Make the decay reach exactly zero at the end of the window ((1 - t/3)² at t = 3) so the process's last frame and the resting ball line up without a jump

Java's ImpulseOperation asks for no repaint during its window, and animationTime() alone never schedules one (EXAMPLES_FINDINGS U6): on the Java player the bounce relies on something else repainting; the C++ and TS players animate it

Canvas coordinates are pixels of the box the host gives the document, not of the header: literal coordinates sit in the top-left and get cut off when it is resized, so scale the drawing to fit (or derive positions from componentWidth()/componentHeight())
